etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English informen, enformen, borrowed from Old French enformer, informer (“to train, instruct, inform”), from Latin īnfōrmō (“to shape, form, train, instruct, educate”), from in- (“into”) + fōrma (“form, shape”), equivalent to in- +‎ form.

definitions.definition: (archaic, transitive) To instruct, train (usually in matters of knowledge).

quote.citation: 1591, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “Prosopopoia. Or Mother Hubberds Tale.”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. […], London:  […]  William Ponsonbie, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: For he would learn their business secretly, / And then inform his master hastily.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene i]:
quote.text: I am informed thoroughly of the cause.

definitions.definition: To act as an informer; denounce.
(transitive) To give form or character to; to inspire (with a given quality); to affect, influence (with a pervading principle, idea etc.).

quote.citation: 2013 June 7, Gary Younge, “Hypocrisy lies at heart of Manning prosecution”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 26, page 18:
quote.text: WikiLeaks did not cause these uprisings but it certainly informed them. The dispatches revealed details of corruption and kleptocracy that many Tunisians suspected, but could not prove, and would cite as they took to the streets.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The Sixth Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 397, lines 1169-1170:
quote.text: Let others better mould the running mass / Of metals, and inform the breathing brass

quote.citation: 1858, Matthew Prior, The poetical works of Matthew Prior, Edinburgh: Printed by Ballantyne and Company, page 120, line 401:
quote.text: O! long as breath informs this fleeting frame / Ne'er let me pass in silence Dorset's name

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To make known, wisely and/or knowledgeably.
(archaic, intransitive) To take form; to become visible or manifest; to appear.

quote.citation: c. 1606 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Macbeth”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: It is the bloody business which informs / Thus to mine eyes.

definitions.definition: Without regular form; shapeless; ugly; deformed.

quote.citation: 1765, Charles Cotton, “Wonders of Peake”, in Poetical Works, page 342:
quote.text: Bleak Crags, and naked Hills, And the whole Prospect so inform and rude
